description: We are interested in Space Mission Design Game.
summary: Mission Island is a browser game in which players design, launch and fly a complete space mission. Each run starts from a real science goal, such as watching wildfires, warning of solar storms, finding ice on the Moon or studying Mars' climate. Players walk a 3D island spaceport and choose the orbit, rocket, spacecraft parts, instruments and ground network. Every choice moves six resources that stay on screen: weight, power, money, data, lifetime and science. A design review blocks any launch that is physically impossible and explains why. The mission then flies day by day, with ageing solar panels, radiation, data backlogs and surprise events based on real NASA cases. On the Moon mission, players drive a rover into a permanently shadowed crater and must get back to sunlight before the battery runs out. Up to four players can share one screen, each with their own role and goal. At the end, a debrief explains what worked and what to fix, and compares the design with real NASA missions. Students learn that every engineering choice affects every other part of a mission.
details:
What it does

Mission Island turns mission design into a loop of decisions that players can try, fail at and improve:

1. Read the mission. Mission Control gives the science goal, the budget, the required lifetime, and the real NASA missions that tackled the same question.

2. Design on the island. There are five buildings, one for each part of a mission. The Launch Complex covers 6 orbits and 4 rockets. The Assembly Hangar covers structure, power, battery, flight computer, pointing system, engine and rover. The Science Lab has 10 instruments. The Ground Station sets the antenna, ground network, relay and observing time. Mission Control runs the design review, which blocks any launch that is physically impossible and offers a Fix button for each problem.

3. Launch. A short launch scene, with real-style rocket reliability.

4. Fly. The mission runs day by day. Solar panels age, radiation strikes and data piles up. Seven kinds of in-flight events appear, each explained with your spacecraft's own numbers and linked to a real event, such as Kepler's reaction wheel failures or the May 2024 geomagnetic storm.

5. Shadowline (Moon mission). Plan and drive a rover route into a permanently shadowed crater near the lunar south pole. The game computes sunlight and Earth line of sight across the terrain. Only data that reaches Earth counts.

6. Debrief. A score out of 1,000 and a grade from S to D, a plain-language report, one concrete tip, and a side-by-side comparison with the closest real NASA mission.

Benefits and impact

Most learning tools teach one topic at a time. Mission Island shows how they connect. A better instrument adds mass, power draw, data and cost. A far orbit weakens sunlight and radio. There is rarely one perfect answer, and the game explains why a design succeeds or fails instead of just marking it right or wrong. We want students to get a feel for real mission trade-offs in about ten minutes and keep coming back to improve their design.

Team play and accessibility

Up to four players share one screen as Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead and Comms & Ops. Each role owns its buildings and has a goal that pulls against the others, and everyone must sign off before launch. The game has 3 difficulty levels, 5 missions plus a Sandbox, plain-word labels, illustrated option cards, a quest guide at the bottom of the screen, per-mission leaderboards, share links for designs, and an in-game helper, Ask CAPCOM, that tests every suggestion in the simulator first.

Tools and technology

Next.js and React (TypeScript and JavaScript), Three.js for the 3D island, launch, orbit and lunar crater, and a deterministic simulation engine that decides every outcome. Orbit periods, speeds and eclipse times are calculated from real gravitational constants and radii. The game is hosted on Vercel from GitHub and runs in any modern browser with nothing to install.

What's next

Real NASA Moon Trek terrain for Shadowline, touch controls, development time as a resource, a class competition mode where teams fly the same mission, and a student playtest.
